FLASHCARD SET · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Places in the Community flashcards.

Twenty-eight places a child’s town is made of, on twenty-eight cards a kid can read. Each card names one place — the library with its open book, the fire station with its truck asleep between the doors, the bakery that smells like tomorrow’s breakfast — and each card page carries a simple guide: who works there, what we do there, and the words to say when we arrive. The town speaks the everyday words of the US, UK and Canada — and where the countries differ (movie theater and cinema, drugstore and chemist’s, gas station and petrol station), both names ride along, so every family hears its own hometown talking.

Every card in the set.

Each card has its own page, and every card shows its age pill — start with the group that fits your child today.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    The Town Walk draw

    Stack the cards face down, draw one, place it at the end of a growing street on the floor, and say what you do there — "at the bakery, I buy bread!" Walk the whole town when the street is finished.

  2. 02

    Same place, two names

    The cards quietly carry both flavors of English: movie theater and cinema, drugstore and chemist’s, gas station and petrol station, shopping cart and trolley. Say both — your child picks a favorite, or keeps both like secrets.

  3. 03

    Before-we-go practice

    Going somewhere today? Pull that card out and talk it through first — the dentist lesson before the check-up, the bus-stop lesson before the first ride. The visit feels half-familiar before you arrive.

  4. 04

    Who works here?

    Lay out four place cards and match the helper to the building: the doctor at the hospital, the librarian at the library, the baker at the bakery, the officer at the police station. Every place has its people.

  5. 05

    The errand map

    Arrange three or four cards in the order of a real errand day — bank, post office, supermarket — and follow the map together, out loud, at home or in the car.

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      School Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Learn, read & imagine

      School is the first place on the tour because your child already owns it: the coat hook, the carpet, the blocks, the door with your name near it. On the card, the schoolhouse stands with its clock on the roof and the flag on top — the building a whole town trusts to raise its children.

      Say it together

      “School! Here is where we learn our letters and our numbers, paint pictures and make friends. The clock on top tells everyone when the school day starts — and when it is time to come home!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play "what comes next": morning carpet, story time, snack, play outside. Line up three toys as a school day and walk a small figure through it — the routine is the lesson.

      Quick parent note

      Every community in the US, UK and Canada runs on its school — it is usually the first public building a child can name. Ask which window might be your child’s classroom; spotting it makes the whole building theirs.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the School lesson on the Learning Path.

      Library Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Learn, read & imagine

      The library is the one store in town where everything is free: shelves of books, story chairs, and a librarian who can find a dragon book in under a minute. On the card, an open book is carved right into the front of the building — the library wears its job on its roof.

      Say it together

      “The library! Shh — here are a thousand books waiting. We pick some, we read them at home, and we bring them back so the next child can borrow them. The open book on the building shows everyone: stories live here!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play library at home: line up books on a couch cushion, make a paper "library card", and take turns being the librarian who stamps the returns. Borrowing and bringing back is the whole game.

      Quick parent note

      A library card is often a child’s first very-own grown-up card, and story times are free in nearly every US, UK and Canadian town. The quiet voice belongs to this place — practicing it is half the fun.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Library lesson on the Learning Path.

      Museum Flashcard for Community

      Ages 4–5Learn, read & imagine

      A museum is a treasure house a whole town agrees to share: dinosaur bones, old trains, paintings bigger than doors. On the card, tall stone columns hold up the front — museums dress like grand palaces because what is inside really is grand.

      Say it together

      “The museum! Inside are old and wonderful things — bones of giant animals, paintings, rockets! We look with our eyes, we walk with quiet feet, and we say "wow" as many times as we want.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Open a home museum: three treasures on a table (a shiny stone, an old key, a feather), paper tickets, and a tour guide who tells one story about each thing. Guides get very dramatic — let them.

      Quick parent note

      Many museums keep free days, and children’s museums are built exactly for four-year-olds who learn by touching. The columns on the card come from ancient Greece — the oldest museum trick in the book.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Museum lesson on the Learning Path.

      Cinema Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Learn, read & imagine

      The cinema is where stories get enormous: the screen taller than the house, chairs in rows, popcorn passed along the row in the dark. On the card, the marquee lights ring the front and the film-reel sign spins its story over the doors.

      Say it together

      “The cinema! We pick our film, we find our seat, the lights go down — hush — and the picture begins, bigger than anything at home! When it ends, the lights come up and we all clap a little.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Home cinema night: dim the lamps, line up the chairs, tickets torn from paper, popcorn in cups. Someone plays the "trailer" by telling tomorrow’s story in a big voice. Lights down, film on.

      Quick parent note

      American families say movie theater; British and Canadian families say cinema — same seats, same popcorn. A child who can sit through a whole film at home is ready for the big dark room; start with a short one.

      Teach it, step by step

      Hospital Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Safe & cared for

      The hospital is the town’s biggest helping place: doctors and nurses, bandages and x-rays, and beds with buttons that move. On the card, a big cross sits on the front — the whole world agrees that this sign means "people who help are inside".

      Say it together

      “The hospital! When someone is hurt or very unwell, we come here, and doctors and nurses know exactly what to do. See the cross on the building? It means: helpers inside!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Treat every toy in the room: one teddy with a sore paw, one dolly with a cough. Bandage with toilet paper, listen with a cardboard-tube stethoscope, and finish every visit with a sticker — hospitals always have stickers.

      Quick parent note

      Knowing the hospital before you need it is the whole trick — a scared first visit is much harder than a familiar one. Most hospitals offer tours, and the teddy-bear clinics many run are exactly for this card.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Hospital lesson on the Learning Path.

      Dentist’s Office Flashcard for Community

      Ages 4–5Safe & cared for

      The dentist’s office is where teeth get their check-ups: a chair that leans back, a little mirror on a stick, and a counter where every brave visit earns a prize. On the card, a giant tooth hangs over the awning — no mistake possible about who works here.

      Say it together

      “The dentist’s office! The dentist counts our teeth — one, two, three — looks for sugar bugs, and polishes until everything shines. Open wide and say ahh! Brave visits get a sticker from the treasure box.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play dentist with a doll: count all the teeth out loud (grown-ups have up to 32!), check with a spoon for a mirror, and brush every single one with an actual toothbrush. The counting IS the check-up practice.

      Quick parent note

      American families say dentist’s office; British families say the dentist’s surgery — same chair, same mirror. The first visits are usually short and friendly on purpose: sit, count, polish, sticker, done.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Dentist’s Office lesson on the Learning Path.

      Pharmacy Flashcard for Community

      Ages 4–5Safe & cared for

      The pharmacy is the quiet helper-shop: hand the prescription over the counter and the pharmacist fills it, counts it, and explains it. On the card, the cross glows above the windows — in many towns the pharmacy is where the lights stay on latest.

      Say it together

      “The pharmacy! The pharmacist takes the paper from the doctor and gives us the medicine that makes us better. Medicine comes from here — and only grown-ups carry it home.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sort the "medicine shelf": colored pom-poms in pill bottles by color and size, labels drawn on, one rule repeated kindly — medicine is only for grown-ups to give. Sorting practice wearing a pharmacist’s coat.

      Quick parent note

      American families say drugstore; British families say chemist’s or pharmacy — the counter works the same in all three. The one safety line rides on this card: medicine is taken only from a grown-up, ever.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Pharmacy lesson on the Learning Path.

      Fire Station Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Safe & cared for

      The fire station is the town’s heroic garage: two big doors, a red truck asleep inside, boots by its side and a pole for sliding down at a moment’s notice. On the card, the truck waits between its doors with the flame badge overhead — ready is the whole job description.

      Say it together

      “The fire station! The firefighters eat, sleep and wait right here — and when the bell rings, WHOOSH, down the pole, on with the boots, and the big red truck roars out to help!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Bell rings, boots on: someone rings an imaginary bell, and the firefighter must put on shoes, hat and "backpack" and run to the door — timed, cheering, again. Ready-in-a-hurry is the game and the real skill.

      Quick parent note

      The truck on the card is American families’ fire truck and British families’ fire engine — same red, same siren. Fire stations are famous for welcoming visits; many give the helmet try-on for free.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Fire Station lesson on the Learning Path.

      Police Station Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Safe & cared for

      The police station never closes: it is where officers start their rounds, where lost things wait to be claimed, and where a child who needs help can knock any hour of the night. On the card, a star sits on a shield — the badge every officer carries matches it.

      Say it together

      “The police station! Police officers keep everyone safe — they help lost children find their grown-ups, they direct traffic, and they work while the whole town sleeps. The star on the badge means: I help!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the friendly-offer game: one toy walks a "street" of cushions and gets lost, and the officer helps by asking questions — what is your name, who are we looking for? Practicing name-and-grown-up is real safety drills in a game.

      Quick parent note

      If your child ever gets lost, the plan in the US, UK and Canada is the same: find a police officer, or a parent with children, and say your name. The card is the friendly version of that lesson — helpers, not fear.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Police Station lesson on the Learning Path.

      Supermarket Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Food & shopping

      The supermarket is the town’s pantry stretched to a building: fruit in pyramids, cereal in towers, a hundred doors of cold air. On the card, the shopping-cart sign rolls over the entrance — everyone who walks in is about to fill something up.

      Say it together

      “The supermarket! We take a cart — some say a trolley — and we fill it with the food for our week. Apples, bread, milk, cheese... what goes in YOUR basket? And at the end, the beeping: beep, beep, beep — all paid!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make a picture shopping list together — five drawings, five finds. Your child holds the list, hunts the shelves, and crosses off every match. The trip stops being "waiting" and becomes a quest.

      Quick parent note

      American and Canadian families push a shopping cart; British families push a trolley — and a store is a shop on the other shore. The whole naming zoo in one card, and both words are correct.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Supermarket lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Bakery Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Food & shopping

      The bakery might be the best-smelling building in town: bread in rows, buns in baskets, and someone in flour who started work before the sun. On the card, the striped awning shades shelves of golden rolls — the windows do the advertising all by themselves.

      Say it together

      “The bakery! Smell that? The baker woke up SO early to bake the bread. We point at what we want — one bun, please! — it goes in the paper bag, still warm, and it never survives the walk home.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Bakery shop at home: play-dough rolls, a paper apron, and customers who order by count — "three buns, please!" Counting out the order is the math; the paper bag is the theater.

      Quick parent note

      A bakery sells bread; a bakeshop or pastry shop leans to cakes — but in every US, UK and Canadian town the corner bakery covers both. If you can, watch the bread being loaded in the morning: it is a free show.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Bakery lesson on the Learning Path.

      Farmers’ Market Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Food & shopping

      The farmers’ market is the supermarket unfolded into the open air: stalls under striped awnings, crates of carrots and greens, and the actual person who grew the tomatoes standing behind them. On the card, the produce piles high — rainbow food, no boxes.

      Say it together

      “The farmers’ market! The farmers bring what they grew — carrots with the green tops still on, corn, berries! We meet the grower, we taste a sample, and the food was in the ground this week.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Market morning game: lay fruits and vegetables on a blanket, assign a farmer and a shopper, and trade with play coins. The farmer must name every crop and answer one question about it ("how do carrots grow?").

      Quick parent note

      Markets run season by season — strawberries in June, squash in October — so the same stall teaches the calendar all year. Many US, UK and Canadian markets double up on kids’ activities; go hungry and go early.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Farmers’ Market lesson on the Learning Path.

      Restaurant Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Food & shopping

      A restaurant is the place where somebody else cooks AND somebody else washes up: a menu to choose from, a table that waits for you, food arriving under a cloche of pure ceremony. On the card, the fork-and-plate sign hangs over the awning — the universal flag for "sit down, someone will come".

      Say it together

      “The restaurant! We sit, we read the menu, we ORDER — "pasta, please!" — and then the waiter brings it, hot from the kitchen. At the end we say thank you, and we do not wash a single dish!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Paper-menu restaurant tonight: draw tonight’s dinner as a menu with pictures, take the order with a notepad, serve with a folded towel over the arm. The waiter role is the prize — fight over who gets it.

      Quick parent note

      Eating out is a skills bundle in disguise: ordering for yourself, waiting for food, saying thank you. In the UK a casual restaurant is often a caff or a bistro; the fork-and-plate sign means the same everywhere.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Restaurant lesson on the Learning Path.

      Pet Shop Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Food & shopping

      The pet shop is the town’s free aquarium: fish weaving in tanks, a dog and a cat watching the street from the window, seed bells and squeak toys in between. On the card, the paw-print sign hangs over the glass — and two furry shopkeepers greet everyone who passes.

      Say it together

      “The pet shop! Look — fish, hamsters, a dog in the window and a cat on a cushion! Every animal here needs food, a bed and a kind family. We can visit the window any day — looking is free.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Pet shop vet day: every stuffed animal in the house goes to the shop for a check-up — weighed, fed a pretend snack, given a paper collar. Then the shop opens and the customer picks a pet to "adopt" — with a promise to feed it forever.

      Quick parent note

      American families say pet store; British families say pet shop — same window, same puppies. A pet shop visit is also the gentlest way to practice the adoption talk: a pet is not a toy, it is a small promise.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Pet Shop lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Bank Flashcard for Community

      Ages 4–5Around the town

      The bank is the town’s treasure room: grown-ups bring their pay here, keep it safe, and take out just enough for the week. On the card, stone columns stand guard and a round coin sits in the roof — banks have looked strong and grand for three thousand years, on purpose.

      Say it together

      “The bank! Grown-ups keep their money here so it is safe. The money machine — the ATM — waits outside, and it gives the right coins any time, day or night. Inside, very big doors keep everything protected.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play bank with a cereal-box teller window: deposits of buttons, withdrawals for "groceries", a receipt scribbled on paper. The piggy bank is the home branch — count the savings, make a deposit, watch it grow.

      Quick parent note

      American families use the ATM; British families say cashpoint or hole-in-the-wall — same machine, same beeping. The card is a first money lesson in disguise: money goes in, money comes out, and saving is the game.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Bank lesson on the Learning Path.

      Post Office Flashcard for Community

      Ages 4–5Around the town

      The post office is the town’s sending place: a parcel on a scale, a stamp in the corner, and a letter that will cross the whole country in somebody’s bag. On the card, a big envelope rides above the doors — the only sign in town that promises a journey.

      Say it together

      “The post office! We write a card, the post officer weighs it — ploop on the scale — we press on a stamp, and off it goes, truck, train, plane, all the way to Grandma’s door!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      The full mail loop at home: write a real letter to someone in the house, stamp it with stickers, deliver it through a door-slot or under a pillow, and wait for the reply. Sending AND receiving — both halves are magic.

      Quick parent note

      The building is the post office everywhere; the street box is a mailbox in the US and Canada and a post box in the UK, and the person is a mail carrier or a postie. One card, four words, all of them true.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Post Office lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Hair Salon Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Around the town

      The hair salon is where the town gets its confidence cut: the scissors-and-comb sign, the swirly wash basin, the big mirror where a brand-new you appears. On the card, the curls and the scissors spell out the promise — everyone walks out standing a little taller.

      Say it together

      “The hair salon! We climb into the big chair, the cape goes on — whoosh — the wash is warm and bubbly, and then: snip, snip, snip! The mirror shows the new haircut, and we say thank you very much!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Salon day for the dolls: a towel cape, a spray bottle wash, a pretend trim, and the all-important mirror reveal with a gasp of admiration. The stylist narrates like an artist — "and NOW... the big finish!"

      Quick parent note

      American families go to the salon or the barber; British families go to the hairdresser’s — same chair, same cape. First haircuts famously come with a certificate and a locked curl of hair; the chair is the milestone.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Hair Salon lesson on the Learning Path.

      Hotel Flashcard for Community

      Ages 4–5Around the town

      A hotel is a whole home folded into one tall building: rooms with beds made by someone else, a desk that hands out keys, three stars promising a good night. On the card, the stars shine over rows of windows — every window is somebody’s room for the night.

      Say it together

      “The hotel! Travelers sleep here when they are far from home. We check in at the desk, we get a key card — beep! — and there is our room: a bed, a window, and tiny bottles of shampoo. Breakfast downstairs!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Home hotel: a suitcase packed for one night in the living room, paper keys handed over the "front desk", room service ( crackers and juice ) ordered by phone. Check out by 11, as the sign says.

      Quick parent note

      British families go on holiday; American and Canadian families go on vacation — and both sleep in hotels. The card teaches the away-from-home routine: check in, sleep, check out, say thank you — portable for life.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Hotel lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Gas Station Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Getting around

      The gas station is the town’s feeding trough for cars: the big canopy, the pumps standing in a row, and the little shop that always has ice cream. On the card, two pumps wait under the roof with a drop sign — to a child, it is simply where the car goes to eat.

      Say it together

      “The gas station! The car is hungry — glug, glug, glug — we feed it gas from the pump, clean the windshield — squeak, squeak — and pay inside. Sometimes the driver of the car gets a snack too!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Car wash and fill-up for ride-ons: chalk prices on paper, a "pump" that counts to ten while filling, windshield wiped with a real cloth. Ten is the magic number — every fill-up is a counting exercise.

      Quick parent note

      American and Canadian families buy gas; British families buy petrol — the station serves both words. The pumps are strictly a grown-up zone, and the card is a good place to say so: look, don’t touch, wait in the car seat.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Bus Stop Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Getting around

      The bus stop is the smallest building in town and one of the most important: a shelter, a bench, a round sign with a bus on it, and a schedule of exactly when the big ride arrives. On the card, the shelter waits with its bench — the whole town passes through it, day after day.

      Say it together

      “The bus stop! We check the time, we wait on the bench, and down the street — here it comes, the big bus! We wave, we climb on, we tap our card, and the driver says good morning. Beep!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Bus route around the house: chairs in a line, tickets torn from paper, stops called at the fridge (Stop 1: Kitchen), the bookshelf (Stop 2: Library) and the bathroom (Stop 3: Splash Pools). Driver rotates every lap.

      Quick parent note

      Waiting in line is a queue in the UK and a line in the US and Canada — both start at a bus stop. Practicing the wait-and-board at home makes the first real ride smooth: bench, wave, tap, sit, ring the bell.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Train Station Flashcard for Community

      Ages 4–5Getting around

      The train station is the town’s thunder room: a clock that rules everything, platforms for every line, and the train itself sliding in with a rush of wind. On the card, the train nose pokes out of the arch under the clock — the clock is not decoration; the whole station obeys it.

      Say it together

      “The train station! We check the big board — platform 2! — we stand behind the yellow line, and HERE IT COMES: whoooosh, the doors slide open, and off we ride, clickety-clack, clickety-clack!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Station at home: the sofa is platform 1, tickets punched with a hole punch, the conductor calls "all aboard!" and clips every ticket. Leave exactly on time — the clock on the card is the boss, and the train waits for nobody.

      Quick parent note

      American families say train station; British families also say railway station — same platforms, same wind. Trains run on the minute, which makes the station a child’s first honest lesson in what a schedule really is.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Train Station lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Airport Flashcard for Community

      Ages 4–5Getting around

      The airport is the town’s door to everywhere: the control tower watching the whole sky, suitcases on parade, and airplanes climbing away over the rooftops. On the card, the pink airplane lifts past the tower — every flight it makes starts and ends in a building exactly like this one.

      Say it together

      “The airport! Suitcases roll, the tower watches the sky, and the airplane takes off — vrrrooom, up up and away! We check in, we wave at the planes, and one day we climb the stairs and fly somewhere wonderful ourselves.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Front-row plane spotting: many airports have a viewing spot where the jets land right over your head. Score each landing, guess the destination from the colors, and practice the wave — every pilot appreciates it.

      Quick parent note

      It is an airplane to American families and an aeroplane to British families — and either way it leaves from the airport. A child who has watched take-offs up close boards their first flight already half an expert.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Community Garden Flashcard for Community

      Ages 4–5Parks & green places

      A community garden is a field chopped into small plots where neighbors grow everything: carrots with the tops on, bean towers, one brave sunflower. On the card, the planter box sprouts carrots and greens — nobody’s garden and everybody’s, at the very same time.

      Say it together

      “The community garden! Everyone in the neighborhood grows something here — carrots, beans, strawberries. We water, we weed a little, we wait... and one day, the very first tomato. Grown by US!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Claim a window box as the family plot: plant radishes or beans (fast, forgiving, exciting to pull up), water on a schedule, and measure the sprout with a paper ruler every Sunday. The wait is the lesson.

      Quick parent note

      The British call their private plot an allotment; the American and Canadian shared version is the community garden — same dirt, same pride. Children who grow a vegetable eat the vegetable: the oldest trick in the parenting book, and it works.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Park Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Parks & green places

      The park is the town exhaling: one enormous tree, a bench in the shade, a lamppost for the evening, and grass that belongs to everyone equally. On the card, the tree does the heavy lifting — parks are measured by their shade, and this one has plenty.

      Say it together

      “The park! Run on the grass, lie under the big tree, listen to the leaves — shhh, shhh. Bring a ball, feed exactly zero pigeons (they prefer it), and rest on the bench with a cold drink. Fresh air is the whole plan.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Meet-a-tree day: pick one tree, learn its bark by hand and its leaves by shape, and visit it every season — spring buds, summer shade, autumn colors, winter branches. One tree makes the whole park personal.

      Quick parent note

      Every US, UK and Canadian town keeps at least one park free for everyone, and the bench is the universal invitation to slow down. The tree on the card is decades old — parks are gifts from townsfolk long gone, kept for the townsfolk still coming.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Playground Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Parks & green places

      The playground is the loudest happy place in town: the slide that ends in a thump and a laugh, the swing that goes higher if you lean right, the ladder that looks taller every winter. On the card, all three ride together — slide, swings and climbing frame — the classic trio.

      Say it together

      “The playground! Up the ladder — step, step, step — sit at the top... and WHEEE, down the slide! Then the swings: lean back, pump the legs, higher, higher! The playground is where the wiggles go to be used up.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Playground circuit: one trip on each thing, then choose a favorite and do it three more times. Teach the two big rules kindly — one at a time on the slide, and wait for the swing to stop before you grab it.

      Quick parent note

      British playgrounds often add a roundabout (the US says merry-go-round), and the see-saw answers to teeter-totter across the border — every town names the same joy differently. Swings are the starter: pumping by yourself is a real independence day.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Recycling Center Flashcard for Community

      Ages 4–5Parks & green places

      The recycling center is the town’s second-chance factory: bottles in one bin, paper in another, cardboard crushed into bales that come back as something new. On the card, the three chasing arrows spin over the doors — reduce, reuse, recycle, in the order the planet prefers.

      Say it together

      “The recycling center! Bottles HERE, paper THERE, cardboard in the middle — crash, clink, stomp! The arrows mean: this is not garbage, this is tomorrow’s something new.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Home sorting line: three boxes for paper, plastic and cans, and a "quality inspector" who checks each item and stamps it through. The inspector role rotates — and the sorting habit sticks for life.

      Quick parent note

      American families carry garbage or trash to the curb; British families carry the rubbish — and the recycling bin is the green one almost everywhere. Kids are famously the strictest sorters in the house; hand them the job and the title.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Sports Center Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Parks & green places

      The sports center is the town’s rain-proof gymnasium: a pool that steams in winter, courts that echo, and a timetable of every game a body can play. On the card, the round window rolls in like a soccer ball — the building plays, too.

      Say it together

      “The sports center! Inside there is a pool, a court, a gym — every game lives here, even when it rains. Bring your shoes, bring your water bottle, and try something new: swimming today, maybe badminton next week!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Family mini-olympics on any flat floor: sock-ball toss into laundry baskets, hallway bowling, a balance-beam line of tape, medal ceremony at the end (paper medals, national anthem optional, absolutely sung).

      Quick parent note

      American families say sports center; British families say leisure centre — same courts, same chlorine smell. Most centers run cheap kids’ swim and soft-play sessions; the timetable is a whole winter’s worth of Tuesdays.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Zoo Flashcard for Community

      Ages 3+Parks & green places

      The zoo is the town’s window into everywhere else on Earth: lions behind the glass, penguins at lunch, the giraffe that looks down at your hat. On the card, the gates stand open under the ZOO sign — inside is the only place a child can meet an elephant before breakfast is over.

      Say it together

      “The zoo! Today we visit the whole world in one walk — the lions, the penguins, the tall tall giraffes! Quiet voices, walking feet, and look who is awake today... every animal has a name plate; we read them together!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Pick three animals before you go — one big, one small, one with a funny name — and make them the quest. Read each name plate out loud: where it lives, what it eats. Three real facts beat a rushed lap of everything.

      Quick parent note

      The zoo is the same word on both shores, but the penguin parade at feeding time is the universal favorite in the US, UK and Canada. The gates on the card open onto the first geography lesson a child ever takes — every animal brings its own map.

      Teach it, step by step
